A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CheckEval, and their complete text, figures, tables and appendices support comparison. The renamed stages and reorganized material can be matched despite substantial expansion.

before.justification: v1 reports original SummEval experiments measuring correlation with human judgments and agreement among GPT evaluators in Section 4 and Tables 1–2.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments across 12 evaluator models on SummEval and Topical-Chat, including agreement, stability, quality-stratified analyses and appendix filtering results.

M1.justification: v1's augmentation procedure expands into independently applied question diversification and elaboration, while author-performed filtering becomes GPT-4o-based filtering (v2 Sections 3.2 and 4.4). These substantially revise checklist construction. Human-defined criteria, Boolean answering and aggregation by the proportion of positive answers remain.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates summarization using SummEval only. v2 additionally evaluates knowledge-grounded dialogue using Topical-Chat, with conversation history, facts and response-quality dimensions including engagingness, groundedness and naturalness. Topical-Chat moves from proposed future work to actual evaluation.

E2.justification: The correlation comparisons remove BLEU and METEOR while retaining ROUGE-L, BERTScore, MoverScore, BARTScore, UniEval and G-Eval. More substantially, v2 introduces G-Eval into the central agreement comparison: v1 Table 2 evaluates CheckEval alone, whereas v2 Tables 3, 12 and 14 directly compare both frameworks.

E3.justification: v1 explicitly samples 10% of SummEval; v2 Section 4.4 describes evaluating all 1,600 samples. The evaluator panel changes from three GPT models to 12 open and closed models. Agreement evaluation adds Krippendorff's alpha and model-group comparisons; new protocols include turn-level dialogue correlations and stratification by human-rated text quality.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's agreement analysis, v2 adds cross-model correlation stability, high- versus low-quality text analysis, and a dialogue case study explaining individual checklist decisions (Section 6). Appendix A adds before/after filtering results. Section 3.3 also reports a pilot comparison of single-question and multi-question inference.

E5.justification: v2 introduces Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction, reported p-values, and cross-model distribution and variance estimates (Table 2, Figure 2 and Table 8). It newly discloses n=1 and fixed seeds. These expand statistical reporting beyond v1's point estimates without establishing increased repeated runs.

E6.justification: The correlation and agreement results are extensively replaced and expanded. For example, the reported GPT-4-turbo SummEval CheckEval Spearman/Kendall row changes from 0.6189/0.4884 in v1 Table 1 to 0.5212/0.4636 under v2's revised setup in Table 11. Changed settings preclude a controlled performance comparison. v2 also adds dialogue, filtering, stability and quality-stratified findings.

T1.justification: Neither version develops substantive theoretical results or proofs. v1's displayed sample-level correlation formula is omitted, but v2 retains the metric in prose. This removes explanatory mathematics rather than changing a theoretical definition or argument; the positive-answer aggregation principle also remains.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes preliminary feasibility, strong human correlation and consistent agreement. v2's abstract, introduction and conclusion assert broader comparative advantages over G-Eval, including reduced cross-model variance and particular effectiveness on high-quality texts. The abstract additionally claims average correlation and agreement improvements of 0.10 and 0.45.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving benchmark–annotation mismatch and uniformly low binary scores on poor responses (Section 6.2). Its limitations discuss mixed-quality long texts, manual checklist-design effort and untested advanced judge methods. These considerably extend v1's future-work discussion of coverage, aggregation and manual filtering.

D1.justification: v2 adds inference temperature and output limits, vLLM 0.6.3, four A100 GPUs, evaluation cost, model identifiers and links, and licenses. Its appendices document generation-stage question counts, both datasets' seed questions and additional prompts. v1 mainly supplies GPT identifiers, final checklist counts and two prompt templates.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated reliability discussion citing Xiao, Bavaresco and Stureborg, acknowledges Ribeiro's CheckList inspiration, and develops positioning around pointwise versus pairwise judging. It also discusses newer decomposition, multi-agent, trained-evaluator and alignment approaches, substantially broadening the research context beyond v1's two related-work subsections.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanation and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The original Case Study and Future Work organization becomes separate Experimental Setup, Results, Analysis and Limitation sections. Terminology changes include aspects to dimensions, key questions to seed questions, and IAA to IEA; title and author information also change.

P2.justification: The workflow is redrawn, incorporating the previously separate aggregation illustration, while v1's introductory evaluator-comparison schematic disappears. v2 adds distribution plots, quality-stratified bar charts and a case-study table. Results use colored model groups and main-text summaries with appendix details; plain prompt tables become expanded colored panels.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited validation: the small SummEval pilot and CheckEval-only agreement analysis become broader experiments with direct G-Eval agreement comparisons, failure analyses and detailed reproduction information. These materially strengthen support for the reliability claims and clarify applicability. Reporting weaknesses remain, including inconsistent metric summaries between Tables 8 and 13 and incorrect dimension headings in Table 14, but the expanded evidence and explicit limitations provide a substantial overall gain.
